newsitem.title: USA: World Bank chief wants to step up loans to Africa.
newsitem.headline: World Bank chief wants to step up loans to Africa.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
World Bank President James Wolfensohn, declaring he was not pessimistic about Africa, said on Wednesday he wanted to step up lending to the region.
"I'm anxious to increase that," he told a news conference before setting out on a nine-day trip to Africa. "We've got money available. What we need are satisfactory projects."
Last year the World Bank approved $2.7 billion in loans for African countries covering 53 projects.
During his nine-day trip that begins Feb. 8, Wolfensohn will visit four countries -- Senegal, Ghana, Mozambique and South Africa.
Arguing that African nations were making real economic progress, Wolfensohn said he wanted to build on that success and discuss ways of promoting foreign investment there.
"Africa is the World Bank's top priority and we want to strengthen our partnerships with the region," he said.
Wolfensohn, who in the past stressed the importance of rooting out corruption in developed and developing countries, made clear he would not be pulling any punches on that issue.
"I will be as always very frank," he said. "Corruption is one of the greatest inhibitors to investors."

Wolfensohn said the World Bank and other financial institutions were pressing ahead with a plan to provide debt relief to the world's poorest nations, many of them in Africa, and that the first case is likely to be taken up by end-April.
"It still looks like Uganda is likely to be the first subject of discussion," he added.

Speaking to reporters in London, British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke named Guyana, Burkina Faso and the Ivory Coast as some of the other countries that might benefit from the debt relief plan.
During his visit to Cape Town, Wolfensohn was expected to discuss granting the Bank's first loan to South Africa.
The loan, which might be on the order of $50 to $60 million, would be targeted at small and medium-sized companies, said Bank Vice President Callisto Madavo.
He told reporters those types of companies have proven successful in other countries in cracking export markets and creating jobs at home.
A decision on the loan could come in few months.
Wolfensohn said the World Bank had not loaned money to South Africa because the country had access to other funding and was not interested.
"It's been their choice," he said. "They don't want any strings tied," he added, referring to the conditions the Bank places on its loans.
